title: Analysing Multitemporal Coherence in Precipitation Patterns Across Different West African Climates
content: This study uses data from the Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station (CHIRPS) over 1981-2024 to examine the temporal and spatial coherence of precipitation regimes in West Africa. Using unsupervised clustering approaches, we distinguished four different precipitation regimes; Wettest, Transitional, Dry, and Very Dry. We compared these regimes to the Köppen climate classification zones to determine how well they corresponded. The study found a moderate correlation (Cramér’s V = 0.224) and a substantial correlation (Chi-square = 86.07, p < 0.0001) between the Köppen classifications and precipitation regimes derived from CHIRPS. Precipitation varies across the Köppen climate classification zones, such as the Tropical Rainforest (Af) and Hot Semi-Arid (BSh), in which drying and recovery were identified using standardised residuals and difference analyses. Conversely, certain zones, such as the Mediterranean, showed surprising classifications that called for further research. Analysis of temporal trends revealed regional variations in precipitation. Significantly, the Tropical Savanna (Aw) and Hot Semi-Arid (BSh) zones showed modest negative trends, indicating possible localised drying. In contrast, the Tropical Monsoon (Am) and Humid Subtropical (Cfa) zones showed positive trends, suggesting a progressive increase in precipitation. These results highlight the value of CHIRPS data in identifying subtle precipitation trends and their correspondence with accepted climatic categories, providing vital information for regional climate assessments and resource management plans.
